title: Two daily rain measures left a 2010-2019 runoff deficit in pre-1997 climate fits at 70 Victorian gauges
abstract: We tested whether daily rain intensity and dry spells account for low runoff after the Millennium Drought. We added the share of annual rain from days with at least 10 mm and the share of days in dry spells of at least seven days to a model with seasonal rain, potential evaporation and three-year climate memory. We used CAMELS-AUS v2.03 and fixed fits before 1997 at 70 Victorian gauges. The 2010-2019 mean residual changed from -0.809 to -0.774 baseline error standard deviations. The paired change was +0.035, with a conditional 95% spatial and time block interval of -0.035 to +0.108. The remaining residual interval was -1.362 to -0.230. At 959 earlier targets in 1982-1996, the added terms raised mean squared log error by 16.08%, with an interval of 1.29% to 32.81%. Checks with SILO rain, stricter flow coverage, square-root runoff and a fixed ridge penalty retained negative residuals. Historical refits also retained a negative residual, but some refits lost matrix rank. This result limits two fixed daily summaries. It does not identify a physical cause or exclude a daily hydrological model. Short records, gridded climate, missing flow, nested gauges, model form and conditional uncertainty limit inference. The package gives code, exact source hashes, aggregate evidence, uncertainty draws, a static figure, a retrieval script and a numerical audit. External record-level data stay outside the signed publication.

display.caption: Daily rain measures left a negative 2010-2019 mean runoff residual in fixed pre-1997 fits. The paired residual change was uncertain. The added terms raised earlier prediction error. Error bars use spatial cells and shared three-year blocks, conditional on fitted models.
